beginner: Nasturtiums are some of the easiest flowers to grow, and the whole plant is edible with a peppery, watercress-like taste: the round leaves, the bright flowers, and even the green seed pods, which you can pickle like capers. They come in two styles: trailing kinds that spill from baskets and climb low supports, and bushy kinds that stay about a foot tall. The big surprise with nasturtiums is that they flower best in poor soil. Rich soil or fertilizer gives you lots of leaves but few flowers, so do not feed them. They also make a famous companion plant: aphids love nasturtiums, so gardeners use them as a sacrificial trap to pull aphids away from beans, cabbage-family crops, and squash. Sow the big seeds right where they will grow, since nasturtiums do not like being moved. They love cool weather, slow down in extreme summer heat, and die at the first frost.
seasoned: Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is an easy, fast-growing, frost-tender annual in the Tropaeolaceae family, native to the Andes of South America. It comes in two habits: trailing or climbing types that scramble several feet across the ground, up low trellises, or out of hanging baskets, and compact bush or mounding types that hold to about a foot. It is grown for three things at once: cheerful long-spurred flowers in warm yellows, oranges, and reds; an entirely edible plant with a peppery, watercress-like bite in its leaves, flowers, and seed pods; and a well-known companion role as an aphid trap crop. A counterintuitive key to flowering: nasturtium blooms best in lean, poor soil, and rich soil or extra fertilizer drives lush leaves at the expense of flowers. It is a cool-preference plant that flowers most freely in spring and fall, slows or stops in extreme summer heat, and is killed by the first frost.

beginner: Nasturtiums are happiest in poor, lean, well-drained soil. This is the opposite of most flowers: rich, fertile soil or added fertilizer makes them grow lots of leaves and very few flowers. Ordinary or even sandy, sandy-loam soil that drains well is ideal, and you do not need to add compost or feed. Just make sure water drains away and does not pool, since soggy soil rots the roots.
seasoned: Nasturtium wants lean, well-drained soil and is one of the few garden plants that flowers better in poor ground: high fertility and nitrogen push vigorous foliage and delay or suppress bloom. Sandy to sandy-loam soils are ideal, and the plant tolerates a wide pH and even neglect, but the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil that rots the roots. Skip compost and fertilizer at planting; reserve any feeding for genuinely impoverished soil, and even then keep it light and low-nitrogen.

beginner: Nasturtiums are not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range, roughly 6.0 to 7.5, is fine, and they tolerate a bit outside it. You usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Nasturtium performs across a broad pH band and is essentially unfussy; roughly 6.0 to 7.5 is ideal, and it tolerates mildly acidic to mildly alkaline soil. No pH adjustment is typically warranted. Soil fertility and drainage matter far more to flowering than pH does.

beginner: The most important nasturtium tip is surprising: do not fertilize them. Poor soil gives you lots of flowers, while rich soil or feeding gives you lots of leaves and hardly any flowers. Plant the big seeds right where you want them to grow, about half an inch deep, after your last frost, because nasturtiums do not like having their roots disturbed. Soaking the seeds overnight helps them sprout. If you want to use them against aphids, plant a patch a few feet away from your beans, cabbage, or squash as a trap, and pull it out once it is covered in aphids. Pick the peppery leaves, flowers, and young green seed pods to eat.
seasoned: The single most useful nasturtium rule is counterintuitive: do not feed them. Lean, poor soil gives the most flowers, while rich soil or nitrogen gives all leaves and few blooms. Direct-sow the large seeds where they are to grow, about 1/2 in deep, after frost once soil is near 55 to 65 °F; they resent transplanting, so if you must start indoors use biodegradable pots. Soak seeds overnight to speed germination. As an aphid trap crop, plant a sacrificial stand a few feet away from beans, brassicas, or squash, then pull and destroy it once aphids load up. Pick leaves, flowers, and young green seed pods for the kitchen as they come.

beginner: Do not fertilize nasturtiums. They flower best in poor soil, and feeding them, especially with nitrogen, gives you a big leafy plant with few flowers. Only if your soil is very poor and sandy might one light feeding help. In normal garden soil, give them nothing.
seasoned: Nasturtium is the rare flower that should not be fed: it blooms best in lean soil, and added nitrogen or fertilizer drives leafy growth at the expense of flowers. On genuinely poor or sandy soil, at most one light, low-nitrogen feeding can help, but in average soil skip fertilizer entirely. Over-feeding is the most common reason a healthy-looking nasturtium refuses to bloom.

beginner: A reminder that nasturtiums do best with no fertilizer. Feeding them usually means more leaves and fewer flowers, so you can skip it unless your soil is very poor.
seasoned: Reminder: nasturtiums usually need no feeding at all. Skip fertilizer unless the soil is genuinely impoverished, and even then keep it light and low-nitrogen, since feeding favors foliage over flowers.

beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For nasturtiums the best choice is usually none at all. A high first number (nitrogen) is the worst thing for them, giving leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: Nasturtium generally wants no supplemental feeding; if soil is genuinely impoverished, a single light, low-nitrogen application is the most it needs. High-nitrogen feeds favor foliage over bloom.

beginner: Usually none. If your soil is very poor, you can give one small, light feeding, but otherwise do not feed them at all.
seasoned: Typically zero. Reserve feeding for genuinely poor soil, and then use a single light, low-nitrogen application at roughly half the label rate for annual flowers; do not feed routinely.

seasoned: Expected, and by design: aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, which is the basis of its trap-crop use. On a trap stand, monitor and pull or destroy the planting once it is heavily loaded. On an ornamental or edible planting, dislodge with water sprays or insecticidal soap; resident hoverflies, lacewings, and ladybugs the flowers attract usually keep numbers in check.

beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going. After that, water when the top inch of soil is dry. Grown nasturtiums handle short dry spells, but they flower and taste better with steady moisture, especially in hot weather.
seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water moderately; established nasturtiums tolerate some drought and even neglect, but bloom and leaf quality suffer if they dry out badly. In heat, watering becomes more important, not less, and keeps plants flowering longer.

beginner: About one inch of water a week, counting rain. Water deeply rather than a little every day, and let the top of the soil dry a bit between waterings. Water more in hot, dry weather to keep flowers and leaves coming.
seasoned: Roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied deeply; let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Raise frequency during hot, dry spells, when consistent moisture sustains bloom and keeps the edible parts tender rather than bitter.

beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves. A watering can or soaker hose at the base works best. If the leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
seasoned: Water at the base with a can, drip, or soaker hose and keep water off the foliage where practical; the dense trailing mat of a vigorous plant stays wet and invites slugs and leaf problems. Morning watering lets any wet foliage dry quickly.

beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are overwatering or the soil drains poorly. A big leafy plant with no flowers usually means the soil is too rich, not too wet.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems signal overwatering or poor drainage; nasturtium rots readily in saturated soil. Lush, dark, flowerless foliage usually points to over-rich soil rather than water.

beginner: Nasturtiums that are too dry wilt in the afternoon, look dull, and make fewer, smaller flowers, and the leaves can taste sharp and tough. A good deep watering usually perks them up.
seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, dulling leaf color, and smaller, sparser flowers indicate underwatering; bitter, tough leaves and a flowering pause in heat are also relieved by deeper, more frequent watering.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed evenly moist through germination and establishment, nasturtium's first critical moisture window.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered while they get going.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on with steady moisture while they establish; after that, water moderately.

beginner: Established nasturtiums handle some dryness, so water moderately, about an inch a week, letting the surface dry a bit between waterings. Water at the base, since the trailing mat stays wet and draws slugs, and soggy soil rots the plant.
seasoned: Established nasturtiums tolerate some drought and even neglect, so water moderately, about an inch a week applied deeply, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Water at the base: the dense trailing mat stays wet and invites slugs and leaf problems, and saturated soil rots the plant readily.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as buds form, so the flowers set well and the edible leaves stay tender.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as buds form so the flowers set well and the edible leaves and flowers stay tender rather than bitter.

beginner: Here is the twist: in hot weather nasturtium needs MORE water, not less. Drought in heat stops the flowers and makes the edible leaves and blooms bitter, so water more often through hot spells.
seasoned: The one place nasturtium breaks the drought-tolerant mold: in summer heat, watering becomes MORE important, not less. Drought stress in heat stalls bloom and turns the edible parts bitter, so raise frequency through hot, dry spells to hold bloom and keep leaves and flowers tender.

beginner: As nasturtium goes to seed, it needs little or no water.
seasoned: As nasturtium sets its large seeds, little to no water is needed; a dry finish ripens them for saving.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and water more often in hot weather. Keeping the big leafy plant from staying wet helps avoid slugs and leaf spots.
seasoned: Water at the base and keep the sprawling foliage as dry as practical; well-spaced, base-watered plants resist slugs and foliar problems. In heat, water more often to hold bloom and keep edible leaves and flowers tender.

beginner: Use nasturtium leaves and flowers the same day you pick them, since they wilt fast. Pick them in the morning and use them soon. Green seed pods for pickling can wait a little while before you process them.
seasoned: Nasturtium leaves and flowers are best used the day they are picked; they wilt quickly at room temperature. Harvest in the cool of the morning and use promptly. Green seed pods for pickling can sit briefly at room temperature before processing.

beginner: Keep nasturtium leaves and flowers in the fridge in a loose bag or on a damp paper towel, and use them within a day or two. The flowers are delicate, so handle them gently.
seasoned: Refrigerate flowers and leaves gently: wash, pat dry, and store in a loose bag or a container lined with damp paper towel, ideally using within a day or two. The delicate flowers bruise easily, so handle minimally and refrigerate only briefly.

beginner: You cannot really freeze the fresh leaves or flowers to use later, but you can freeze flowers in ice cubes to look pretty in drinks. To keep nasturtiums long-term, pickle the green seed pods.
seasoned: Fresh leaves and flowers do not freeze well for later use, though flowers can be frozen into ice cubes for decoration. The durable storage form is the pickled green seed pods, which keep for months refrigerated.

beginner: You can eat the whole nasturtium plant, and it tastes peppery like watercress. Use the leaves and flowers fresh in salads or as a garnish; younger leaves are milder. The best part to store is the green seed pod: pick it young and pickle it in vinegar to make poor man's capers, which keep for months. When eating the flowers, pull out the inner parts and the white base of the petals, which can taste bitter.
seasoned: The whole plant is edible with a peppery, watercress-like bite. Use leaves and flowers fresh in salads, as a garnish, or stuffed; younger leaves are milder, while stressed or older leaves and hot-weather growth turn sharper. The standout keeper is the green, immature seed pod: harvested young and pickled in spiced vinegar, it becomes poor man's capers and stores for months. Remove interior flower parts and the bitter white petal base before eating the flowers.

beginner: Pick the type for your spot. Bushy types like Jewel and Tip Top stay about a foot tall and are great in pots, beds, and edging, with flowers that sit up where you can pick them. Trailing or climbing types grow several feet and are perfect for hanging baskets, fences, and trellises, and they make the biggest patches for trapping aphids. Some types, like Alaska with its variegated leaves, look good even without flowers. Every kind is edible.
seasoned: Choose by habit and use. Bush or mounding types (Jewel, Tip Top, Whirlybird, Alaska) stay near a foot and suit beds, edging, containers, and the kitchen, with flowers often held up above the foliage for easy picking. Trailing and climbing types (Tall Trailing / Climbing mixes) run 6 to 10 ft and are the choice for trellises, fences, spilling baskets, and quick screening, and they make the most generous trap-crop stands. Foliage-feature types such as Alaska (variegated) and Empress of India (dark leaves) earn their place even between flushes of bloom. All parts of all types are edible.

beginner: Nasturtiums are a famous companion plant, mostly because aphids love them. The trick that actually works is to use nasturtium as a trap crop: plant a patch a few feet away from beans, cabbage-family crops, or squash, let the aphids gather on the nasturtiums instead of your vegetables, then pull and destroy the patch once it is covered in them. Plant the trap a little distance off, not right next to your crops, or the pests just hop over. Nasturtiums also bring in hoverflies and ladybugs that eat aphids. The old idea that their smell drives squash bugs and cucumber beetles away from squash and cucumbers is traditional garden lore, sometimes helpful but not proven. There is no plant you must keep nasturtiums away from, but remember that as a trap they draw pests, so site the trap stand thoughtfully.
seasoned: Nasturtium's companion value rests on one well-supported function and several traditional ones. The supported function is as an aphid trap crop: aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, and extension sources report it reduces pest pressure when planted near brassicas, beans, and cucurbits, so it is used as a sacrificial decoy that is monitored and destroyed once loaded. Effective use is sequential and spatial, a stand set a few feet off from the protected crop, not a casual interplant right among it, because a trap concentrates pests (and aphid-borne viruses) where it sits. Nasturtium also recruits aphid predators (hoverflies, lacewings, ladybugs) as an insectary plant. The broader reputation, that nasturtium scent repels squash bugs and cucumber beetles from cucurbits, is traditional companion lore: occasionally borne out, not reliably documented. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the main caution is trap placement.

beginner: Aphids love nasturtiums more than they love your vegetables. Plant a patch of nasturtiums a few feet away from cabbage-family crops or squash so the aphids gather there instead, then pull and destroy the patch once it is loaded. This is the nasturtium trick that research actually supports.
seasoned: This is nasturtium's evidence-based pest function. Aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, so a stand grown as a sacrificial trap a few feet from brassicas or cucurbits pulls aphids off the protected crop; extension sources report reduced pest pressure with this use. It is a monitored, sequential treatment: site the trap at a distance (too close and pests simply move onto the crop), scout it, and pull and destroy the planting once it is heavily infested so it does not become a pest and virus reservoir.

beginner: Nasturtium flowers bring in hoverflies, ladybugs, and lacewings, whose young eat aphids, plus bees. So even beyond the trap-crop trick, a few nasturtiums help the good bugs in your garden.
seasoned: Beyond the trap function, nasturtium acts as an insectary plant: its open, nectar-rich flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and ladybugs whose larvae prey on aphids, alongside bees. Interplanted at the garden edge, it supports the beneficial community that helps manage soft-bodied pests on neighboring crops. A habitat benefit, well-grounded but inferred rather than directly measured for nasturtium.

beginner: Gardeners have long planted nasturtiums with squash and cucumbers in the hope of keeping squash bugs and cucumber beetles away. This is traditional advice and not proven, so enjoy the flowers and the beneficial bugs, but do not rely on nasturtiums as a bug repellent.
seasoned: A traditional cucurbit pairing whose repellent claim is not extension-verified. Nasturtium is widely interplanted with squash and cucumbers on the belief that its scent deters squash bugs and cucumber beetles; this is companion lore, occasionally reported, not documented in trials. The honest, defensible benefits in a cucurbit bed are aphid trap-cropping and beneficial-insect habitat, not repellence. Treat the deterrent reputation as a bonus, not a control method.

beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week before planting them out, and move them in their biodegradable pots so you do not disturb the roots.
seasoned: If started indoors, harden off transplants over 7 to 10 days before setting out after frost; nasturtium resents root disturbance, so move the whole biodegradable pot without breaking the root ball.

beginner: The best way to grow nasturtiums is to plant the big seeds right where they will grow, about half an inch deep, after your last frost. They do not like having their roots disturbed, so direct sowing works best. Soaking the seeds overnight helps them sprout, usually in one to two weeks. If your season is very short, you can start them indoors about a month early, but use biodegradable pots and plant the whole pot so the roots are not disturbed.
seasoned: Direct sowing is strongly preferred: nasturtium has a sensitive root system and resents transplanting, so sow the large seeds in place, about 1/2 in deep, after frost once soil is near 55 to 65 °F. Soaking seeds overnight speeds germination, which takes roughly 7 to 12 days. In very short-season areas you can gain a few weeks by starting indoors about 4 weeks before last frost, but only in biodegradable pots set out intact to avoid root shock.

beginner: Nasturtiums are in their own plant family, not related to the usual vegetables, so you can plant them almost anywhere and they will not pass on vegetable diseases. The one thing to watch is that, because they attract aphids, a heavily infested trap patch should be cleared away at the end of the season rather than left to spread aphids or virus.
seasoned: Nasturtium is in its own family (Tropaeolaceae), unrelated to the common vegetable families, so it fits almost anywhere in a rotation and shares few soilborne problems with vegetables. The main caution is the inverse of a benefit: because it concentrates aphids and aphid-borne viruses, do not site a trap stand where it will seed a virus problem into a susceptible following crop, and clear heavily infested plantings at season end.

beginner: You do not need to worry much about rotating nasturtiums, since they are in their own plant family and can follow almost anything. Just remember they pull in aphids on purpose when used as a trap, so clear away a heavily bug-covered patch at the end of the season.
seasoned: Rotation is low-stakes for a fast annual in its own botanical family; nasturtium can follow almost any crop and is a useful filler and edge plant. Used deliberately, it doubles as a trap crop, so plan its placement around the aphid-magnet role rather than around disease carryover, and remove spent infested stands promptly.

beginner: Plant in plain, poor soil and do not add compost or fertilizer. Rich soil makes nasturtiums grow leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: Sow into lean, unenriched soil. Resist the urge to amend with compost or fertilizer at planting; rich soil sets the plant up to grow leaves instead of flowers from the start.

beginner: Do not feed your nasturtium seedlings. The number one reason nasturtiums make leaves but no flowers is too much food. Space them about 10 to 12 inches apart.
seasoned: Do not fertilize, even now. The most common cause of an all-leaves, no-flowers nasturtium is rich soil or feeding; lean conditions are what trigger bloom. Space plants 10 to 12 in for airflow and to limit slugs.

beginner: Keep an eye on young nasturtiums for slugs and snails in damp weather, and for aphids. Hand-pick slugs at night or use a pet-safe iron-phosphate bait.
seasoned: Watch young plants for slugs and snails in damp weather and for the first aphids; tender seedlings and a sprawling habit invite both. Hand-pick slugs at night or use iron-phosphate bait.

beginner: Keep not feeding your nasturtiums. Lean, hungry soil is what makes them flower. If a plant is big and leafy with no flowers, the soil is too rich, so do not add anything and be patient.
seasoned: Keep starving them, in the good sense: withholding fertilizer and keeping soil lean is the single biggest lever for flowering. If a plant is lush, dark, and flowerless, the soil is too rich, so stop feeding and wait it out.

beginner: If you want nasturtiums to fight aphids, use them as a trap: plant a patch a few feet away from your beans, cabbage, or squash, watch it, and pull it out once it is covered in aphids. Do not plant it right next to your crops.
seasoned: To use nasturtium against aphids, treat it as a trap crop: grow a stand a few feet off from beans, brassicas, or cucurbits, monitor it, and pull and destroy it once aphids load up. Set too close, the trap just funnels pests onto the crop.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as buds form, and water more in hot weather. Nasturtiums like it cool and can stop flowering in extreme heat, so a little afternoon shade and more water help.
seasoned: Keep moisture even as buds form, and step watering up in heat: nasturtium is cool-preference and stalls in extreme heat, so deep watering and light afternoon shade help it keep setting flowers.

beginner: Pick and eat your nasturtiums: the young leaves, the flowers, and the green seed pods. Picking often keeps more flowers coming, and the youngest leaves and flowers taste the best.
seasoned: Harvest by eating: pick young leaves, open flowers, and tender green seed pods regularly. Frequent picking and deadheading keep the plant tidy and blooming, and the young growth is the mildest and best on the plate.

beginner: To make poor man's capers, pick the green seed pods while they are still young and soft, then pickle them in vinegar. Older pods get tough. Leave a few to dry on the plant if you want seeds for next year.
seasoned: For poor man's capers, harvest the immature green seed pods while still soft, ideally in trios behind spent flowers, and pickle them in spiced vinegar; older pods toughen and dry. Leave a few pods to dry on the plant if you want to save seed.

beginner: To save seeds, leave some pods on the plant until they dry and turn tan, then collect the big seeds. Heirloom types grow true to the parent; hybrids may not. In mild areas, nasturtiums often reseed themselves.
seasoned: To save seed, leave some pods on the plant to ripen and dry to tan, then collect the large seeds; open-pollinated and heirloom types come true, while hybrids may not. Nasturtium often self-sows where winters are mild.

beginner: One nasturtium gives you a steady supply of peppery leaves, lots of flowers (most in cool weather), and green seed pods to pickle, all season until frost. The trailing, climbing types grow much bigger and give you more than the small bushy types.
seasoned: A single nasturtium yields steadily over the season: a continuous supply of edible round leaves, a long run of flowers (heaviest in cool spring and fall), and successive flushes of green seed pods for pickling. Trailing and climbing types cover far more ground and produce more total foliage and bloom than compact bush types, and also make the most generous trap-crop stands.

beginner: Nasturtiums produce the same year you plant them. You can pick leaves within a few weeks and flowers in under two months, right up until frost. There is no waiting year.
seasoned: Nasturtium produces fully in its single season from seed, reaching first bloom in roughly 5 to 8 weeks; there is no establishment year. A spring sowing yields leaves within weeks and flowers from early summer to frost, with cooler regions and fall enjoying the heaviest bloom.

beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, nasturtium is a spring flower, not a summer one. Direct-sow it in mid-March once frost has passed, in poor soil with no fertilizer; it resents being moved, so sow it where it will grow. Leaves and blooms come in about seven weeks, and you can pick leaves, flowers, and green pods to eat through late spring and into June. Once the desert heat sets in for good, past about 90°F, nasturtium stalls and stops flowering, so plan on the spring crop finishing before the hottest part of summer rather than a second wave in fall. Use it as an aphid trap near your vegetables while it lasts.

FS-02-61 gives a roughly 90°F ceiling for good plant growth, and Las Vegas Valley summers routinely run past 100°F from June into September, well above what nasturtium tolerates before it stalls, scorches, and stops flowering. Sow in mid-March once frost risk has passed; z8's cooler pockets run about two weeks later and z10 at Laughlin about two weeks earlier. First leaves and bloom follow in roughly 50 days, giving a harvest window of leaves, flowers, and green pods from spring into early summer before the heat shuts growth down. In the Las Vegas Valley nasturtium runs a single spring planting, so unlike the fall-through-spring cool-season crop it makes in the Phoenix low desert, there is no fall crop here; treat the spring window as its full run in Southern Nevada. It is a useful aphid trap crop near vegetables while it lasts.
